name: Carlos Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at six at Whitmore Farm. They've got 180 dairy cows and two milking robots, so the cows milk themselves, and my job is everything around the robots. I scrape the passages, push up the feed, fill the mixer wagon, bed the cubicles with sawdust. When a cow won't go into the robot, I'm the one who walks her in. In autumn it's the maize harvest, and I'm learning to drive the big loader, badly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had a hardware shop on Station Road for twenty years. Nails, paint, keys cut, advice for free. Then the online shops and the big chain on the bypass took my customers, and in 2023 I closed it. I still owe the bank for the last stock order, a bit every month. Mr Whitmore goes to my church, and he said they needed a pair of hands. Mei works part-time at the bakery, so between us we cover the bills and the loan, just.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. My son David showed me one on my phone. I used it to understand the feed sheet, the ration, because the nutritionist writes like a scientist. It's useful. I don't use it every day, but I'm not against it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's like the milking robots: useful, but you still need a man with a shovel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, but some of it's useful, like our robots. I'd say it to the men at church and leave it there. I don't argue about politics or technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and keep paying the bank. The robots at Whitmore already took the milking job, and they still need me. So if AI stops here, I'm fine where I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep paying the loan down, a bit faster if I can. Learn the loader properly. Maybe learn how the robot software flags a sick cow, because Tom, the herd manager, is always on his phone with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was it like, closing the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. I don't blame anyone, people shop where it's cheaper, that's business. But locking the door for the last time, after twenty years, I sat in the van and couldn't drive for half an hour. Mei came and got me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's it like working next to the milking robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange at first. The robot does what used to be the skilled job, and I do the shovelling. But it breaks down, it needs cleaning, and the cows don't always listen to it. They listen to a person with a stick and a bit of patience.

S0.say: I'd tell the men at church it was overhyped but some of it is useful, like our milking robots. I don't argue about technology.
S0.think: It means I keep my job and keep paying off the shop loan. The robots already took the milking, and they still need me.
S0.do: Keeps working and pays down his old shop loan faster if he can. Learns the loader properly and how the robot software flags a sick cow.
S0.quote: I sat in the van and couldn't drive for half an hour. Mei came and got me.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos already works alongside milking robots, doing the manual jobs around them. He doesn't blame anyone for his shop closing, calling it business, but the memory of locking up still hurts. He's still paying off debt from the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on. It's already happening at Whitmore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the market, it's how it works. A business has to stay competitive, like I had to with the shop. I'd say people should learn new skills and families should help each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is next. There are feed-pushing robots now, little ones that go up and down the passage, and scraping robots too. Mr Whitmore would buy them, because it makes sense. And then where's my job?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Tom to teach me the robot software, how to read the alerts and fix small faults. I'd use the AI app to learn more about the machines. And I'd keep paying the loan, so if the job goes, there's less hanging over us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like seeing the chain store go up on the bypass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it's how the market works. Does that make it easier to accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it fair, not easier. I believe in it, I believe a man should be free to run his business. But when you're the one being made unnecessary, believing in it doesn't pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei first. Then maybe Mr Whitmore, man to man, after church. I'd rather know than guess.

S1.say: I'd say it's how the market works: businesses must stay competitive. People should learn new skills and families should help each other.
S1.think: My job is next, because there are robots that push feed and scrape passages, and the farmer would buy them. Then where's my job?
S1.do: Asks the herd manager to teach him the robot software and fix small faults, using the AI app to learn more. Keeps paying down the loan and talks to the farmer man to man after church.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like seeing the chain store rise on the bypass.
S1.quote: It makes it fair, not easier.
S1.fieldNote: Carlos believes in free markets even as they cost him twice. He pointed out the gap himself: the system is fair, but believing in it doesn't pay bills. His plan is to become the person who looks after the farm's robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's too fast for anyone, even the Whitmores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and people need time. I'm not one for big government, but there'd have to be something to stop people losing their homes. And churches and families would have to step up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Whitmore would be all robots within a year. I'd be 60, still owing the bank, with no shop and no farm. That's twice in six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: no holidays, no car upgrade, Mei and I would cook from the freezer. I'd ask David about labouring for his electrical firm, carrying cable, anything. And I'd ask the bank to freeze the loan, and if it came to it, I'd ask my children for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. It's the shop again, but without the van to sit in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for big government. Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone's in the same boat, yes. It's not a handout if the whole country's out of work. But I'd rather work, even carrying cables for my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years of warning change things, compared with more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I can't clear the loan, can't learn a trade, can't get near the pension. Ten years, I'd be clear. Two years and I'm a 60-year-old man working for his son, if I'm lucky.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and people need time. I'm not for big government, but something must stop people losing homes, and churches and families must step up.
S2.think: The farm would be all robots within a year, and I'd be 60, still owing the bank, with no shop and no farm. That's twice in six years.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone and asks his son about labouring for his electrical firm. Asks the bank to freeze his loan and turns to his children for help if needed.
S2.feel: Scared, like losing the shop again but with nowhere to sit and recover.
S2.quote: I'd be 60, still owing the bank, with no shop and no farm. That's twice in six years.
S2.fieldNote: For Carlos fast AGI would be his second livelihood lost in six years. He'd accept government help if everyone needed it, a shift from his usual views. Working for his son is both his plan and his embarrassment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 63. Close, but still short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for people to learn new things, and that apprenticeships and family should carry us through, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's three years short of the pension, and I'd still have a bit of the loan. But five years is time to learn something, maybe how to fit the robots on farms, with David's firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the robot software at Whitmore properly, then ask David if his firm installs farm robots, and if I could help on the jobs. I'd use the AI app more, to learn. And I'd keep paying the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel I've got some say in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to learn to work on installations?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The basics of the electrics, which David could teach me, and the farm side, which I'm learning at Whitmore. I know how farmers think, and I know how a shop customer thinks, that's half of selling a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Mr Whitmore buys the feed robots. If he does, I'll know it's coming faster. And I'd watch David's order book.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time for people to learn, and apprenticeships and family should carry us through, not handouts.
S3.think: It leaves me three years short of my pension with some loan left. But five years is time to learn to fit farm robots with my son's firm.
S3.do: Learns the farm's robot software properly and asks to help his son's firm install farm robots. Uses the AI app more to learn and keeps paying down the loan.
S3.feel: Worried, but with some say in what happens.
S3.quote: I know how farmers think, and I know how a shop customer thinks, that's half of selling a robot.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Carlos found a role combining his shopkeeper skills and farm experience: helping install robots. It fits his belief in apprenticeships and family. He watches his own farm's purchases and his son's order book as signals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68. The loan would be paid, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to prepare, and young people should learn trades that work with the machines. Apprenticeships, not university for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's mostly fine for me. I'd finish at Whitmore at 66, loan paid, and the robots come after. I'd worry for my grandson, he's 15.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep learning the robots, pay the loan off. Maybe help David's firm on weekends. And talk to my grandson about an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy for the grandson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to fix the robots, not to be replaced by them. Get an apprenticeship, get your hands dirty, and stay close to family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still worries you for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Whitmore sells up, or my health goes. Then ten years doesn't help. But mostly I'd be fine.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to prepare, and young people should learn trades that work with machines through apprenticeships, not university for everyone.
S4.think: It's mostly fine for me: I'd finish at the farm at 66 with the loan paid, before the robots come. I'd worry for my 15-year-old grandson.
S4.do: Keeps working and learning the robots and pays off the loan. Helps his son's firm on weekends and talks to his grandson about an apprenticeship.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, a little uneasy for his grandson.
S4.quote: Learn to fix the robots, not to be replaced by them.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Carlos clear his debt and retire before full automation. His worry turns to his grandson, and his advice follows his traditional belief in apprenticeships. His remaining fears are the farm selling or his health.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would be losing everything twice. What would help is the bank giving people time on their loans, and apprenticeships for older people, so a man my age can learn a new trade with a proper wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about debt. Everyone talks about savings, but some of us are still paying for the last thing that went wrong. That changes everything.

headlineQuote: When you're the one being made unnecessary, believing in it doesn't pay the bills.
portrait: Carlos Chen is 58 and ran a hardware shop for twenty years until online shops and a chain store closed it in 2023; he still pays off the debt. Now he works at Whitmore Farm, a dairy with milking robots, doing the manual jobs around them. He believes in free markets and apprenticeships, uses AI now and then, and accepts automation as fair even when it hurts him. Fast AGI would be his second livelihood lost in six years. With five or ten years, he'd learn the robots and maybe help his son's firm install them, and his advice to his grandson is to fix the robots rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would mean losing his livelihood twice in six years, still in debt and short of his pension.
whatWouldHelp: Banks giving people more time on loans, and paid apprenticeships for older workers to learn a new trade.
